div.head: 379. Memorandum of Conversation

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: President’s Meeting with Ecuadorean President-elect Leon Febres Cordero
Secretary of State George P. Shultz
Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs Langhorne A. Motley
Mr. Robert C. McFarlane, National Security Council
RADM John M. Poindexter, Deputy Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs
Constantine Menges, Senior Director, Latin American Affairs, NSC

div.p: President Reagan welcomed the President-elect and congratulated him on his recent electoral victory. The President said that Vice President Bush would represent him at the August 10 inauguration in Quito.

Febres Cordero thanked the President and explained that he had campaigned on the same policies as President Reagan—i.e., use of the market to set prices. He then explained how Ecuador’s economic condition had worsened since 1979 when the country had returned to democracy from military rule. The size of the, budget, the deficit, the rate of inflation, the number of public sector employees and the external debt were all much greater today than five years ago. The Febres Cordero government has the political will to make the necessary changes to correct this situation, but they will need help from the US, he said. If the new government fails in Ecuador, the democratic system will fail. The new government takes office with a 100,000 vote margin of victory, but this could easily change. If the government succeeds, an historic victory will have been achieved and Ecuador can become the showplace for American democracy.

President Reagan responded that we wish to help, but we also have constraints. Secretary Shultz added that Peter McPherson has been discussing ways in which PL–480 and our housing program can be used early in the new administration to provide a political offset to politically difficult actions such as major increases in gasoline prices. President Reagan continued that the deterioration in such matters as the size of the budget and inflation had occurred in the US as it had in Ecuador. One of the successes of this Administration had been to reduce the inflation rate to 1/3 of what it had been earlier. The biggest improvement, however, had been in putting people to work. Six million jobs have been created in the last 18 months through the activities of free enterprise.

The Ecuadorean President-elect outlined Ecuador’s difficulty in servicing its external debt. The country exports approximately $2.5 billion a year. In 1979, 15% of exports were used to service the debt. Now interest alone consumes 40% of exports. Yesterday’s rise of 1/2% in the US prime rate will cost Ecuador approximately $35 million.

President Reagan responded that the high interest rates are a great frustration to him and that he believes the problem is mainly psychological. The financial community still does not believe that the Administration will not revert to inflationary policies. The government does have control, President Reagan said, and he is mad about the bank actions.
Vice President Bush pointed out that Febres Cordero will be meeting tonight with the major international banks and the President-elect said that he would pass on the President’s thoughts.
The meeting closed with Febres Cordero’s extension of best wishes to President Reagan in the upcoming US elections. He said that the western world needs President Reagan’s leadership.
The Vice President will represent the President at the August 10 inauguration in Quito.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, George P. Shultz Papers, Box 47F, Latin America. Confidential. The meeting took place in the Oval Office. No drafting information appears on the memorandum.
Febres-Cordero won the May 6 election. See Alan Riding, “Businessman Wins in Ecuador Vote,” New York Times, May 7, 1984, p. A13.

In message WH6462 to the Department of State and the Embassy in Ecuador, August 13, the White House sent a summary of Bush’s August 11 meeting with Febres-Cordero at the Ecuadorian Presidential Palace. (George H.W. Bush Library, Bush Vice Presidential Records, Office of National Security Affairs, Donald P. Gregg Files, OA/ID 19809–016, Foreign Travel Files, 19809–016, Vice President’s Trip to Ecuador, August 10–11, 1984: Memcons) Reagan’s August 8 congratulatory letter to Febres-Cordero is in the Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Country File, Ecuador (07/15/1984–04/02/1985).

In telegram 190917 to Quito, June 29, the Department reported on Shultz’s June 6 meeting with President-elect Febres-Cordero, writing: “The Secretary told President-elect Febres Cordero that the United States will work for the success of its free market approach to Ecuador’s development. Febres said he hopes to end the government’s practice of subsidizing prices in his country but wants to move concurrently to provide food and housing. On relations with the communists, Febres declared that he has warned both the Cuban and Soviet Ambassadors that they must behave.” The Department also reported that McPherson, who attended the meeting, “expressed the hope that the USG can help through the housing investment guarantee program. We hope to be able to dedicate PL 480 proceeds to housing, McPherson continued. The creation of employment and visible housing would give political cover to measures such as raising gasoline prices.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840417–0818)
